title: Following a frame from the network to the screen

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Picture a video stream with a perfectly healthy bitrate that still feels late. The numbers look fine, and your thumbs disagree. So where did the time go?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That's a sneaky one. If the speed looks fine, where do you even start looking?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's the question behind Artemis Switch, Antoine's fork of Moonlight-Switch, a game streaming client for the Nintendo Switch. He focuses on the short trip between receiving a frame and putting it on screen, and asks where each frame waited.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So the PC does the heavy lifting, and the Switch just shows the result?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly. A PC running Sunshine or Apollo sends the game over the Moonlight protocol. On the Switch, the video is decoded with FFmpeg and NVDEC, lands in a small queue, and a graphics layer called deko3d presents it. The client owns everything from that queue onward, so it's easy to tell whose job a hiccup is.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Like a restaurant kitchen. Plates come out, wait at the pass, then a server carries them to the table.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Great picture, and the pass is where Antoine's clever part lives. When frames pile up, the client decides which to keep. It checks the deadline of the oldest frame first, and once the queue is ready, it drops older frames and shows the freshest.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Why the oldest frame instead of just the newest?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: If the gate chased the newest arrival, its deadline would keep sliding forward. Frames would keep coming in, but nothing would be shown. Anchoring on the oldest deadline keeps the screen moving, and a backlog can skip the usual wait so a slow renderer catches up.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And how do you know it's working?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A small telemetry piece times each stage separately: decode, queue wait, render, GPU submission, the real video bitrate, and milestones like first packet and first presented frame. It uses a monotonic clock, so timings stay steady.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So instead of one vague latency number, you get a timeline for each frame.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. The app also offers Fit, Fill and Stretch modes, FSR-style upscaling with sharpening, named stream profiles and a performance overlay. Keep the host, scene and network fixed, change one option at a time, and compare queue wait and present intervals, handheld and docked separately.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: A neat habit for any pipeline.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly: don't ask how fast the decoder is, ask where each frame waited. The full write-up has the pipeline diagram and the source links.
